
## Ecosystem Projections

```{r cover-ceilings}
# z-log scale ceilings corresponding to 100% benthic cover.
# Both cover equations were fitted with trunc(ub = z_ceil) to respect the
# 0–100% biological bound. The same ceiling is applied in all projection
# matrices so that manual propagation is consistent with the SEM likelihood.
# Values are hardcoded (verified: back-transform to exactly 100% cover).
z_ceil_coral  <- 3.39   # (log(100) - mean(log(coral%))) / sd(log(coral%))
z_ceil_fleshy <- 2.26   # (log(100) - mean(log(fleshy%))) / sd(log(fleshy%))
```

```{r full-sem-proj-data}
#| label: full-sem-proj-data
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Compute full-SEM projection matrices — needed by the reduced SEM comparison plot.

# ── Projection years (standardised to SEM scale) ─────────────────────────────
proj_years <- 2005:2055
year_std   <- (proj_years - modelmean$Year) / modelsd$Year

# 3 000 thinned posterior draws
set.seed(7341)
post <- as_draws_df(brms_sem_full) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  slice_sample(n = 3000)

n <- nrow(post)
p <- length(proj_years)

# Helper: multiply each row of an (n × p) matrix by a length-n coefficient vector
rs <- function(coef, mat) sweep(mat, 1, coef, "*")
yr_mat <- matrix(rep(year_std, each = n), nrow = n)  # n × p

# ── Propagate causal chain through the full SEM ───────────────────────────────
# 1. Temperature (z-scored)
temp_mat <- rs(post$b_temperature_Year, yr_mat) + post$b_temperature_Intercept

# ── yearresid matrix: observed z-scaled values for hindcast (2005–2025),
#    0 (standardised mean) for forecast years (2026–2055). yearresid captures
#    year-specific temperature anomalies beyond the linear trend; setting it to 0
#    for forecast years assumes future deviations are unknown and average out.
obs_yr_actual   <- round(semdata2$Year * modelsd$Year + modelmean$Year)
yr_resid_lookup <- tibble(Year = obs_yr_actual, yr = semdata2$yearresid)
yr_resid_vec    <- sapply(proj_years, function(y) {
  row <- yr_resid_lookup |> filter(Year == y)
  if (nrow(row) == 1 && !is.na(row$yr)) row$yr else 0
})
yr_resid_mat <- matrix(rep(yr_resid_vec, each = n), nrow = n)

# 2. Coral cover (log-standardised; temperature + yearresid predictors)
coral_mat <- rs(post$b_logcoral_temperature, temp_mat)    +
             rs(post$b_logcoral_yearresid,   yr_resid_mat) +
             post$b_logcoral_Intercept

# 3. Ecosystem respiration (coral + direct temp via bsp for mi() imputed predictor)
rd_mat <- rs(post$b_logrd_logcoral,          coral_mat) +
          rs(post$bsp_logrd_mitemperature,   temp_mat)  +
          post$b_logrd_Intercept

# 4. Fleshy macroalgae (log-standardised; coral predictor)
fleshy_mat <- pmin(rs(post$b_logfleshy_logcoral, coral_mat) + post$b_logfleshy_Intercept,
                   z_ceil_fleshy)

# 5. Corallivore fish (z-scored; coral predictor)
cov_mat <- rs(post$b_Corallivore_logcoral, coral_mat) + post$b_Corallivore_Intercept

# 6. Herbivore fish (z-scored; fleshy algae predictor)
herb_mat <- rs(post$b_herbs_logfleshy, fleshy_mat) + post$b_herbs_Intercept

# 7. Ecosystem Pmax (log-standardised; rd + coral + temp, all via bsp/b)
pmax_mat <- rs(post$bsp_logpmax_milogrd,      rd_mat)    +
            rs(post$b_logpmax_logcoral,        coral_mat) +
            rs(post$bsp_logpmax_mitemperature, temp_mat)  +
            post$b_logpmax_Intercept

# 8. Algal N content (log-standardised; rd via bsp imputed)
n_mat <- rs(post$bsp_Npercent_milogrd, rd_mat) + post$b_Npercent_Intercept

# ── Back-transform to original units ─────────────────────────────────────────
bt_log <- function(mat, mu, sig) exp(mat * sig + mu)
bt_lin <- function(mat, mu, sig) mat * sig + mu

proj_list <- list(
  Temperature    = bt_lin(temp_mat,   modelmean$temperature, modelsd$temperature),
  `Coral Cover`  = bt_log(coral_mat,  modelmean$logcoral,    modelsd$logcoral),
  Respiration    = bt_log(rd_mat,     modelmean$logrd,       modelsd$logrd),
  `Fleshy Algae` = bt_log(fleshy_mat, modelmean$logfleshy,   modelsd$logfleshy),
  Pmax           = bt_log(pmax_mat,   modelmean$logpmax,     modelsd$logpmax),
  # N_percent is log-transformed in semdata2; use explicit log-scale params
  `N Content`    = bt_log(n_mat,
                          mean(log(Year_Averages$N_percent), na.rm = TRUE),
                          sd(log(Year_Averages$N_percent),   na.rm = TRUE))
)

# Derive P:R ratio directly from back-transformed Pmax and Rd matrices
proj_list[["P:R Ratio"]] <- proj_list$Pmax / proj_list$Respiration

# ── Summarise: posterior median + 50% + 95% CI per variable per year ─────────
proj_tbl <- imap_dfr(proj_list, function(mat, vname) {
  tibble(variable = vname,
         Year     = rep(proj_years, each = n),
         value    = as.vector(mat)) |>
    group_by(variable, Year) |>
    summarise(median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
              lo95   = quantile(value, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE), hi95 = quantile(value, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE),
              lo50   = quantile(value, 0.25,  na.rm = TRUE), hi50 = quantile(value, 0.75,  na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop")
})

# ── Observed data for overlay ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
obs_proj <- Year_Averages |>
  transmute(Year,
            Temperature    = Max_temp,
            `Coral Cover`  = mean_coral,
            Respiration    = Rd,
            `Fleshy Algae` = mean_fleshy,
            Pmax           = Pmax,
            `N Content`    = N_percent,
            `P:R Ratio`    = Pmax / Rd) |>
  pivot_longer(-Year, names_to = "variable", values_to = "observed")
```

## Reduced SEM: Parsimonious Model

Three of the twelve pathways in the full SEM had 95% credible intervals spanning zero — direct temperature effects on respiration (β = 0.22, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.62), direct temperature effects on Pmax (β = −0.16, −0.78 to 0.45), and a direct coral effect on Pmax (β = −0.35, −1.40 to 0.71) — indicating that these pathways are not reliably supported by the data. Retaining them in projection creates two problems: the positive temperature→Rd coefficient generates a spurious upward push on Rd when temperature is extrapolated beyond the fitted range, and the large uncertainty on the coral→Pmax and temperature→Pmax terms inflates Pmax credible intervals. A reduced 9-pathway SEM was therefore fitted with these three terms removed.

```{r sem-reduced-fit}
#| label: sem-reduced-model
#| cache: true

# Reduced SEM: remove 3 non-significant pathways
#   1. Temperature → Rd (direct):      remove mi(temperature) from bf_logrd
#   2. Temperature → Pmax (direct):    remove mi(temperature) from bf_logpmax
#   3. Coral → Pmax (direct):          remove logcoral from bf_logpmax

bf_temp_r        <- bf(temperature | mi()             ~ 1 + Year)
bf_coraltemp_r   <- bf(logcoral    | trunc(ub = 3.39) ~ 1 + temperature + yearresid +
                         ar(time = Year, p = 1))
bf_logrd_r       <- bf(logrd       | mi()             ~ 1 + logcoral)
bf_logpmax_r     <- bf(logpmax     | mi()             ~ 1 + mi(logrd))
bf_fleshy_r      <- bf(logfleshy   | trunc(ub = 2.26) ~ logcoral)
bf_herbs_r       <- bf(herbs       | mi()             ~ 1 + logfleshy)
bf_corallivore_r <- bf(Corallivore | mi()             ~ 1 + logcoral)
bf_nutrients_r   <- bf(Npercent    | mi()             ~ 1 + mi(logrd))

brms_sem_reduced <- brm(
  bf_temp_r + bf_coraltemp_r + bf_logrd_r + bf_herbs_r + bf_corallivore_r +
    bf_nutrients_r + bf_fleshy_r + bf_logpmax_r + set_rescor(FALSE),
  data    = semdata2,
  chains  = 3, iter = 10000, warmup = 5000, seed = 11,
  sample_prior = "no",
  prior   = c(
    set_prior("normal(0, 2)",    class = "b"),
    set_prior("normal(0, 2)",    class = "Intercept"),
    set_prior("normal(0, 0.25)", resp = "temperature", class = "sigma", lb = 0),
    set_prior("normal(0, 0.5)",  class = "ar",  resp = "logcoral")
  ),
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 15),
  family  = gaussian(),
  silent = 2, refresh = 0
)
```

```{r sem-reduced-summary}
#| label: sem-reduced-results

summary(brms_sem_reduced)
```

```{r sem-reduced-r2}
#| label: sem-reduced-r2

# Manual R² for mi()-imputed responses
for (resp in c("logrd", "logpmax")) {
  fit_f <- fitted(brms_sem_full,    resp = resp)[, "Estimate"]
  fit_r <- fitted(brms_sem_reduced, resp = resp)[, "Estimate"]
  obs_v <- semdata2[[resp]]
  ok    <- !is.na(obs_v)
  cat(sprintf("%-10s  Full R²: %.3f   Reduced R²: %.3f\n", resp,
              cor(fit_f[ok], obs_v[ok])^2, cor(fit_r[ok], obs_v[ok])^2))
}
```

```{r sem-reduced-projections}
#| label: reduced-sem-projection-data

set.seed(6214)
post_r <- as_draws_df(brms_sem_reduced) |> as_tibble() |> slice_sample(n = 3000)
n_r    <- nrow(post_r)

# yearresid matrix: observed for 2005-2025, zero for 2026-2055
yr_resid_vec_r <- sapply(proj_years, function(y) {
  row <- yr_resid_lookup |> filter(Year == y)
  if (nrow(row) == 1 && !is.na(row$yr)) row$yr else 0
})
yr_resid_mat_r <- matrix(rep(yr_resid_vec_r, each = n_r), nrow = n_r)
yr_mat_r       <- matrix(rep(year_std, each = n_r), nrow = n_r)

# ── Propagate reduced SEM causal chain ────────────────────────────────────────
temp_mat_r   <- rs(post_r$b_temperature_Year,     yr_mat_r)   + post_r$b_temperature_Intercept
coral_mat_r  <- rs(post_r$b_logcoral_temperature, temp_mat_r) +
                rs(post_r$b_logcoral_yearresid,   yr_resid_mat_r) +
                post_r$b_logcoral_Intercept
rd_mat_r     <- rs(post_r$b_logrd_logcoral, coral_mat_r)      + post_r$b_logrd_Intercept
fleshy_mat_r <- pmin(rs(post_r$b_logfleshy_logcoral, coral_mat_r) + post_r$b_logfleshy_Intercept,
                     z_ceil_fleshy)
cov_mat_r    <- rs(post_r$b_Corallivore_logcoral, coral_mat_r)+ post_r$b_Corallivore_Intercept
herb_mat_r   <- rs(post_r$b_herbs_logfleshy, fleshy_mat_r)    + post_r$b_herbs_Intercept
pmax_mat_r   <- rs(post_r$bsp_logpmax_milogrd, rd_mat_r)      + post_r$b_logpmax_Intercept
n_mat_r      <- rs(post_r$bsp_Npercent_milogrd, rd_mat_r)     + post_r$b_Npercent_Intercept

proj_list_r <- list(
  Temperature    = bt_lin(temp_mat_r,   modelmean$temperature, modelsd$temperature),
  `Coral Cover`  = bt_log(coral_mat_r,  modelmean$logcoral,    modelsd$logcoral),
  Respiration    = bt_log(rd_mat_r,     modelmean$logrd,       modelsd$logrd),
  `Fleshy Algae` = bt_log(fleshy_mat_r, modelmean$logfleshy,   modelsd$logfleshy),
  Pmax           = bt_log(pmax_mat_r,   modelmean$logpmax,     modelsd$logpmax),
  `N Content`    = bt_log(n_mat_r,
                          mean(log(Year_Averages$N_percent), na.rm = TRUE),
                          sd(log(Year_Averages$N_percent),   na.rm = TRUE))
)
proj_list_r[["P:R Ratio"]] <- proj_list_r$Pmax / proj_list_r$Respiration

proj_tbl_r <- imap_dfr(proj_list_r, function(mat, vname) {
  tibble(variable = vname, Year = rep(proj_years, each = n_r), value = as.vector(mat)) |>
    group_by(variable, Year) |>
    summarise(median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
              lo95 = quantile(value, .025, na.rm = TRUE), hi95 = quantile(value, .975, na.rm = TRUE),
              lo50 = quantile(value, .25,  na.rm = TRUE), hi50 = quantile(value, .75,  na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop")
})

# ── Counterfactual: temperature stabilised at 2025 ────────────────────────────
# temp_2025_std: z-standardised 2025 annual maximum temperature
# = (observed 2025 max temp - SEM temperature mean) / SEM temperature SD
# Use last non-NA Max_temp as the counterfactual (2025 is NA)
temp_2025_val <- Year_Averages |>
  filter(!is.na(Max_temp)) |>
  slice_max(Year, n = 1) |>
  pull(Max_temp)
temp_2025_std <- (temp_2025_val - modelmean$temperature) / modelsd$temperature
temp_mat_r_cf <- temp_mat_r
temp_mat_r_cf[, which(proj_years > 2025)] <- temp_2025_std

coral_mat_r_cf  <- rs(post_r$b_logcoral_temperature, temp_mat_r_cf)   +
                   rs(post_r$b_logcoral_yearresid,   yr_resid_mat_r)  +
                   post_r$b_logcoral_Intercept
rd_mat_r_cf     <- rs(post_r$b_logrd_logcoral, coral_mat_r_cf)        + post_r$b_logrd_Intercept
fleshy_mat_r_cf <- pmin(rs(post_r$b_logfleshy_logcoral, coral_mat_r_cf) + post_r$b_logfleshy_Intercept,
                        z_ceil_fleshy)
pmax_mat_r_cf   <- rs(post_r$bsp_logpmax_milogrd, rd_mat_r_cf)        + post_r$b_logpmax_Intercept
n_mat_r_cf      <- rs(post_r$bsp_Npercent_milogrd, rd_mat_r_cf)       + post_r$b_Npercent_Intercept

proj_tbl_r_cf <- imap_dfr(
  list(Temperature    = bt_lin(temp_mat_r_cf,   modelmean$temperature, modelsd$temperature),
       `Coral Cover`  = bt_log(coral_mat_r_cf,  modelmean$logcoral,    modelsd$logcoral),
       Respiration    = bt_log(rd_mat_r_cf,     modelmean$logrd,       modelsd$logrd),
       `Fleshy Algae` = bt_log(fleshy_mat_r_cf, modelmean$logfleshy,   modelsd$logfleshy),
       Pmax           = bt_log(pmax_mat_r_cf,   modelmean$logpmax,     modelsd$logpmax),
       `N Content`    = bt_log(n_mat_r_cf,
                               mean(log(Year_Averages$N_percent), na.rm = TRUE),
                               sd(log(Year_Averages$N_percent),   na.rm = TRUE))),
  function(mat, vname) {
    tibble(variable = vname, Year = rep(proj_years, each = n_r), value = as.vector(mat)) |>
      group_by(variable, Year) |>
      summarise(median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
                lo95 = quantile(value, .025, na.rm = TRUE), hi95 = quantile(value, .975, na.rm = TRUE),
                lo50 = quantile(value, .25,  na.rm = TRUE), hi50 = quantile(value, .75,  na.rm = TRUE),
                .groups = "drop")
  })

```

## Copernicus CDS CMIP6 SST Projections to 2100

```{r cds-setup}
#| label: cds-setup
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# ── Run once to store your CDS Personal Access Token securely ─────────────────
# 1. Log in at https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/
# 2. Go to Profile (top-right) → Personal Access Tokens → copy your token
# 3. Paste it below and run this chunk once — it will not need to be run again.
library(ecmwfr)
wf_set_key(key = "YOUR-PERSONAL-ACCESS-TOKEN")
```

```{r cds-cmip6-sst-download}
#| label: cds-cmip6-sst-download
#| cache: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false

# ── Download CMIP6 sea surface temperature (tos) from Copernicus CDS ──────────
# Five coupled ScenarioMIP models confirmed to have tos for historical (1950–2014)
# and all three needed SSPs (2015–2100) in the CDS projections-cmip6 dataset:
# ACCESS-CM2, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-LR, UKESM1-0-LL.
# Monthly resolution, spatially subsetted to a 3° box around Moorea LTER Site 1
# (~17.5°S, 149.8°W).
#
# IMPORTANT: CDS returns only one model per request when multiple are listed —
# requests are therefore submitted one per model × experiment (20 total).
# With workers = 2, expect ~40–60 minutes on first run.

library(ecmwfr)

sst_dir     <- here("data", "cmip6_sst")
all_months  <- as.list(sprintf("%02d", 1:12))
moorea_area <- c(-16.0, -151.0, -19.0, -148.0)

# Models confirmed viable on CDS for all required experiments
viable_models <- c("access_cm2", "ipsl_cm6a_lr", "miroc6", "mpi_esm1_2_lr", "ukesm1_0_ll")

# Map CDS snake_case names → NC filename fragment for existence check
model_nc_name <- c(
  access_cm2    = "ACCESS-CM2",
  ipsl_cm6a_lr  = "IPSL-CM6A-LR",
  miroc6        = "MIROC6",
  mpi_esm1_2_lr = "MPI-ESM1-2-LR",
  ukesm1_0_ll   = "UKESM1-0-LL"
)

experiments_cfg <- list(
  list(exp = "historical",  years = 1950:2014),
  list(exp = "ssp1_2_6",    years = 2015:2100),
  list(exp = "ssp2_4_5",    years = 2015:2100),
  list(exp = "ssp5_8_5",    years = 2015:2100)
)

# Create experiment output directories
for (exp_cfg in experiments_cfg)
  dir.create(file.path(sst_dir, exp_cfg$exp), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Build pending requests: skip any model-experiment whose NC already exists
pending_requests <- list()
for (exp_cfg in experiments_cfg) {
  exp_dir <- file.path(sst_dir, exp_cfg$exp)
  for (model_name in viable_models) {
    nc_present <- any(grepl(model_nc_name[[model_name]],
                            list.files(exp_dir, pattern = "\\.nc$")))
    if (!nc_present) {
      pending_requests <- c(pending_requests, list(list(
        dataset_short_name  = "projections-cmip6",
        temporal_resolution = "monthly",
        experiment          = exp_cfg$exp,
        variable            = "sea_surface_temperature",
        model               = list(model_name),
        year                = as.list(as.character(exp_cfg$years)),
        month               = all_months,
        area                = moorea_area,
        target              = sprintf("tos_%s_%s.zip", model_name, exp_cfg$exp)
      )))
    }
  }
}

if (length(pending_requests) > 0) {
  message(sprintf("Submitting %d CDS requests (one per model × experiment)...",
                  length(pending_requests)))
  wf_request_batch(pending_requests, workers = 2, path = sst_dir)

  # Extract each per-model zip to its experiment directory
  for (exp_cfg in experiments_cfg) {
    exp_dir <- file.path(sst_dir, exp_cfg$exp)
    for (model_name in viable_models) {
      zip_path <- file.path(sst_dir, sprintf("tos_%s_%s.zip", model_name, exp_cfg$exp))
      if (file.exists(zip_path))
        unzip(zip_path, exdir = exp_dir, overwrite = FALSE)
    }
  }
} else {
  message("All model NC files already present — skipping CDS download.")
}
```

```{r cds-cmip6-sst-process}
#| label: cds-cmip6-sst-process
#| cache: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false

# ── Read CDS NetCDF files, extract Moorea grid cell, bias-correct ─────────────
# Produces:
#   wb_proj_bc   — ensemble p10/median/p90 per scenario-year (used in propagation)
#   ann_cmip6_bc — per-model historical annual max SST (used for spread ribbon)

library(ncdf4)

sst_dir    <- "data/cmip6_sst"
moorea_lon <- -149.83
moorea_lat <- -17.48

# Extract model name from CMIP6 standard filename:
# <var>_<freq>_<model>_<exp>_<variant>_<grid>_<period>.nc
extract_model_name <- function(filepath) {
  parts <- strsplit(basename(filepath), "_")[[1]]
  if (length(parts) >= 3) parts[3] else "unknown"
}

read_tos_nc <- function(nc_path, experiment) {
  nc <- nc_open(nc_path)
  on.exit(nc_close(nc))

  model <- extract_model_name(nc_path)

  # Coordinates — handle 1-D regular, 2-D curvilinear, and NEMO (nav_lon/nav_lat) grids
  lon <- tryCatch(ncvar_get(nc, "lon"),
           error = \(e) tryCatch(ncvar_get(nc, "longitude"),
             error = \(e2) ncvar_get(nc, "nav_lon")))
  lat <- tryCatch(ncvar_get(nc, "lat"),
           error = \(e) tryCatch(ncvar_get(nc, "latitude"),
             error = \(e2) ncvar_get(nc, "nav_lat")))

  # Normalise 0–360 longitudes to -180–180
  lon_norm <- ifelse(lon > 180, lon - 360, lon)

  if (length(dim(lon)) == 2) {
    # Curvilinear grid
    dist  <- sqrt((lon_norm - moorea_lon)^2 + (lat - moorea_lat)^2)
    idx   <- which(dist == min(dist, na.rm = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)
    tos_raw <- ncvar_get(nc, "tos")[idx[1, 1], idx[1, 2], ]
  } else {
    i_lon   <- which.min(abs(lon_norm - moorea_lon))
    i_lat   <- which.min(abs(lat      - moorea_lat))
    tos_raw <- ncvar_get(nc, "tos")[i_lon, i_lat, ]
  }

  # Time → calendar dates
  time_raw   <- ncvar_get(nc, "time")
  time_units <- ncatt_get(nc, "time", "units")$value
  origin_str <- sub("^days since ", "", time_units)
  dates      <- as.Date(origin_str) + as.integer(round(time_raw))

  # Replace fill values with NA
  fv <- ncatt_get(nc, "tos", "_FillValue")$value
  if (length(fv) > 0) tos_raw[abs(tos_raw - fv) < abs(fv) * 1e-3] <- NA

  # Convert Kelvin → Celsius if needed
  u <- ncatt_get(nc, "tos", "units")$value
  if (length(u) > 0 && grepl("^K$|kelvin", u, ignore.case = TRUE))
    tos_raw <- tos_raw - 273.15

  n <- min(length(dates), length(tos_raw))
  tibble(model      = model,
         experiment = experiment,
         date       = dates[seq_len(n)],
         tos        = as.numeric(tos_raw[seq_len(n)]))
}

# Read NC files directly from pre-extracted experiment directories.
# (The download chunk extracts each per-model zip to its experiment directory,
# so no unzipping is needed here.)
all_tos <- map_dfr(c("historical", "ssp1_2_6", "ssp2_4_5", "ssp5_8_5"),
  function(experiment) {
    exp_dir  <- file.path(sst_dir, experiment)
    nc_files <- list.files(exp_dir, pattern = "\\.nc$", full.names = TRUE)
    if (length(nc_files) == 0) { warning("No NC files in: ", exp_dir); return(NULL) }
    map_dfr(nc_files, \(f) tryCatch(
      read_tos_nc(f, experiment),
      error = \(e) { warning(basename(f), ": ", e$message); NULL }
    ))
  })

# Annual maximum SST per model-year
ann_tos <- all_tos |>
  mutate(year = year(date)) |>
  group_by(model, experiment, year) |>
  summarise(ann_max = max(tos, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(is.finite(ann_max))

# ── Delta bias correction: anchor each model to observed MCR 2005-2025 mean ───
obs_mean_mcr_cds <- mean(Year_Averages$Max_temp[Year_Averages$Year %in% 2005:2025],
                         na.rm = TRUE)

bias_tbl_cds <- ann_tos |>
  filter(
    (experiment == "historical"                            & year %in% 2005:2014) |
    (experiment %in% c("ssp1_2_6","ssp2_4_5","ssp5_8_5") & year %in% 2015:2025)
  ) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(model_mean = mean(ann_max, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(bias = obs_mean_mcr_cds - model_mean)

ann_tos_bc <- ann_tos |>
  left_join(bias_tbl_cds, by = "model") |>
  mutate(ann_max_bc = ann_max + bias)

# ── Ensemble p10 / median / p90 per experiment-year ───────────────────────────
ens_stats <- function(data, exp_name) {
  data |>
    filter(experiment == exp_name) |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(p10    = quantile(ann_max_bc, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE),
              median = quantile(ann_max_bc, 0.50, na.rm = TRUE),
              p90    = quantile(ann_max_bc, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(experiment = exp_name)
}

ssp_ens  <- bind_rows(
  ens_stats(ann_tos_bc, "ssp1_2_6"),
  ens_stats(ann_tos_bc, "ssp2_4_5"),
  ens_stats(ann_tos_bc, "ssp5_8_5")
)
hist_ens <- ens_stats(ann_tos_bc, "historical")

# ── Build wb_proj_bc (structure expected by downstream propagation code) ───────
ssp_long <- ssp_ens |>
  pivot_longer(c(p10, median, p90), names_to = "percentile", values_to = "tasmax_bc") |>
  mutate(scenario = case_when(
    experiment == "ssp1_2_6" ~ "ssp126",
    experiment == "ssp2_4_5" ~ "ssp245",
    experiment == "ssp5_8_5" ~ "ssp585"
  )) |>
  select(year, scenario, percentile, tasmax_bc)

# Historical 2005-2014 expanded across all three scenarios for the overlap window
hist_long <- hist_ens |>
  filter(year %in% 2005:2014) |>
  pivot_longer(c(p10, median, p90), names_to = "percentile", values_to = "tasmax_bc") |>
  select(year, percentile, tasmax_bc) |>
  expand_grid(scenario = c("ssp126", "ssp245", "ssp585"))

wb_proj_bc <- bind_rows(hist_long, ssp_long) |>
  distinct(year, scenario, percentile, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  arrange(scenario, percentile, year) |>
  filter(year %in% 2005:2100)

# ── ann_cmip6_bc: historical per-model series for the 2005-2014 spread ribbon ─
ann_cmip6_bc <- ann_tos_bc |>
  filter(experiment == "historical")
```

```{r wb-cmip6-propagate}
#| label: wb-cmip6-propagate

# ── Propagate each SSP scenario through the reduced SEM ──────────────────────
# Approach: two uncertainty sources are kept separate.
#
#   Temperature panel  — shows the raw CMIP6 inter-model spread (p10/p90 of
#     the 10 bias-corrected models). This ribbon is NOT derived from the SEM.
#
#   Ecological panels  — driven by a single, deterministic ensemble-median
#     temperature trajectory per scenario. All 3,000 SEM posterior draws use
#     identical temperatures, so the ribbon reflects SEM path-coefficient
#     uncertainty only (not climate-model structural uncertainty). This keeps
#     the two sources of uncertainty clearly interpretable and the ecological
#     ribbons clean.
#
# yearresid uses observed values for 2006–2025 (captures the 2010 cyclone/
# bleaching trajectory and other non-temperature secular trends), tapered
# linearly to zero by 2035.

# ── Map scenario codes to experiment names used in ann_tos_bc ────────────────
ssp_experiment <- c(ssp126 = "ssp1_2_6", ssp245 = "ssp2_4_5", ssp585 = "ssp5_8_5")

# Build a bias-corrected model × year temperature matrix for a given scenario
get_model_temp_matrix <- function(scenario_name) {
  exp_name <- ssp_experiment[[scenario_name]]

  temps <- bind_rows(
    ann_tos_bc |> filter(experiment == "historical", year %in% 2005:2014),
    ann_tos_bc |> filter(experiment == exp_name,     year %in% 2015:2100)
  ) |>
    select(model, year, ann_max_bc)

  # Retain only models with a complete, non-missing 96-year series
  complete_models <- temps |>
    group_by(model) |>
    summarise(n = n(), ok = all(!is.na(ann_max_bc)), .groups = "drop") |>
    filter(n == 96L, ok) |>
    pull(model)

  temps |>
    filter(model %in% complete_models) |>
    arrange(model, year) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = ann_max_bc) |>
    select(-model) |>
    as.matrix()                          # n_complete_models × 96
}

# ── CMIP6 ensemble temperature summary (for Temperature panel display) ────────
# Returns median, p10, and p90 across models for each scenario/year.
get_temp_ensemble_summary <- function(scenario_name) {
  temp_raw <- get_model_temp_matrix(scenario_name)   # n_models × 96 (2005:2100)

  # Historical (2005–2025): observed MCR temperatures, zero ribbon — mirrors the
  # two-period approach used for ecological variables so all panels are consistent.
  hist_rows <- Year_Averages |>
    filter(Year %in% 2005:2025) |>
    arrange(Year) |>
    transmute(
      scenario = scenario_name,
      variable = "Temperature",
      year     = Year,
      median   = Max_temp,
      lo95     = Max_temp, hi95 = Max_temp,
      lo50     = Max_temp, hi50 = Max_temp
    )

  # Projection (2026–2100): CMIP6 ensemble median + p10/p90 inter-model spread
  proj_rows <- tibble(
    scenario = scenario_name,
    variable = "Temperature",
    year     = 2026:2100,
    median   = apply(temp_raw[, 22:96, drop = FALSE], 2, median),
    lo95     = apply(temp_raw[, 22:96, drop = FALSE], 2, quantile, 0.10),
    hi95     = apply(temp_raw[, 22:96, drop = FALSE], 2, quantile, 0.90),
    lo50     = apply(temp_raw[, 22:96, drop = FALSE], 2, quantile, 0.25),
    hi50     = apply(temp_raw[, 22:96, drop = FALSE], 2, quantile, 0.75)
  )

  bind_rows(hist_rows, proj_rows)
}

# ── SEM propagation for ecological variables ──────────────────────────────────
# Two-period approach matching the reference figure design:
#
#   2005–2025  → observed ecosystem values used directly (median = observed;
#                lo95 = hi95 = median → no ribbon). The SEM's yearresid
#                coefficients applied on top of CMIP6 temperatures give
#                historically inconsistent predictions; bypassing the SEM here
#                yields lines that track the observed open circles.
#
#   2026–2100  → Delta-method anchoring on the observed 2025 state.
#                For each posterior draw, compute the SEM's predicted *change*
#                from its own 2025 baseline (using CMIP6 T_2025 + yearresid_2025)
#                and add that delta to the observed 2025 z-score. This removes
#                SEM level bias while preserving scenario-specific trends, and
#                guarantees continuity at the 2026 boundary. yearresid is held
#                constant at its 2025 value so that projected changes reflect
#                only CMIP6 temperature anomalies (tapering yearresid to zero
#                would spuriously relieve secular decline pressure on coral).
propagate_wb_ssp <- function(scenario_name) {

  n_pct_log_mean <- mean(log(Year_Averages$N_percent), na.rm = TRUE)
  n_pct_log_sd   <- sd(log(Year_Averages$N_percent),   na.rm = TRUE)

  # ── CMIP6 ensemble-median temperature trajectory ──────────────────────────
  temp_raw     <- get_model_temp_matrix(scenario_name)
  temp_med_raw <- apply(temp_raw, 2, median)               # length 96 (2005:2100)
  temp_z_cmip6 <- (temp_med_raw - modelmean$temperature) / modelsd$temperature

  cmip6_z_2025 <- temp_z_cmip6[21]                         # index 21 = year 2025
  tm_proj      <- matrix(rep(temp_z_cmip6[22:96], each = n_r), nrow = n_r)  # n_r × 75

  # ── yearresid: held constant at its 2025 observed value ──────────────────
  # The yearresid captures secular (non-temperature) trends up to 2025. For
  # the projection period we hold it constant rather than tapering to zero:
  # tapering would gradually relieve the downward pressure on coral, producing
  # a spurious recovery signal unrelated to temperature forcing. Holding it
  # constant ensures projected changes are driven purely by CMIP6 temperature
  # anomalies relative to the 2025 baseline.
  yr_2025 <- {
    row <- yr_resid_lookup |> filter(Year == 2025L)
    if (nrow(row) == 1L && !is.na(row$yr)) row$yr else 0
  }
  yr_rv_proj <- rep(yr_2025, 75)   # constant at 2025 level throughout projection
  yrm_proj   <- matrix(rep(yr_rv_proj, each = n_r), nrow = n_r)

  # ── SEM baseline at 2025 (CMIP6 T_2025 + observed yearresid_2025) ────────
  cm_base  <- pmin(post_r$b_logcoral_temperature * cmip6_z_2025 +
                   post_r$b_logcoral_yearresid   * yr_2025 +
                   post_r$b_logcoral_Intercept, z_ceil_coral)          # n_r
  rm_base  <- post_r$b_logrd_logcoral          * cm_base + post_r$b_logrd_Intercept
  fm_base  <- pmin(post_r$b_logfleshy_logcoral * cm_base +
                   post_r$b_logfleshy_Intercept, z_ceil_fleshy)
  pm_base  <- post_r$bsp_logpmax_milogrd  * rm_base + post_r$b_logpmax_Intercept
  nm_base  <- post_r$bsp_Npercent_milogrd * rm_base + post_r$b_Npercent_Intercept

  # ── SEM projection at 2026–2100 ───────────────────────────────────────────
  cm_proj  <- pmin(rs(post_r$b_logcoral_temperature, tm_proj) +
                   rs(post_r$b_logcoral_yearresid,   yrm_proj) +
                   post_r$b_logcoral_Intercept, z_ceil_coral)
  rm_proj  <- rs(post_r$b_logrd_logcoral,          cm_proj) + post_r$b_logrd_Intercept
  fm_proj  <- pmin(rs(post_r$b_logfleshy_logcoral, cm_proj) +
                   post_r$b_logfleshy_Intercept, z_ceil_fleshy)
  pm_proj  <- rs(post_r$bsp_logpmax_milogrd,  rm_proj) + post_r$b_logpmax_Intercept
  nm_proj  <- rs(post_r$bsp_Npercent_milogrd, rm_proj) + post_r$b_Npercent_Intercept

  # ── Observed z-scores at 2025 (anchor points) ────────────────────────────
  obs25 <- Year_Averages |> filter(Year == 2025)
  obs_cm_z <- (log(obs25$mean_coral)  - modelmean$logcoral)  / modelsd$logcoral
  obs_rm_z <- (log(obs25$Rd)          - modelmean$logrd)     / modelsd$logrd
  obs_fm_z <- (log(obs25$mean_fleshy) - modelmean$logfleshy) / modelsd$logfleshy
  obs_pm_z <- (log(obs25$Pmax)        - modelmean$logpmax)   / modelsd$logpmax
  # N_percent: use last non-NA year if 2025 is missing
  n_anchor <- if (!is.na(obs25$N_percent)) obs25$N_percent else {
    Year_Averages |> filter(!is.na(N_percent)) |> slice_max(Year, n = 1) |> pull(N_percent)
  }
  obs_nm_z <- (log(n_anchor) - n_pct_log_mean) / n_pct_log_sd

  # ── Delta-anchored projection matrices ───────────────────────────────────
  # anchored[draw, year] = obs_z_2025 + (proj[draw, year] - base[draw])
  cm_anch <- pmin(sweep(cm_proj, 1, cm_base, "-") + obs_cm_z, z_ceil_coral)
  rm_anch <- sweep(rm_proj, 1, rm_base, "-") + obs_rm_z
  fm_anch <- pmin(sweep(fm_proj, 1, fm_base, "-") + obs_fm_z, z_ceil_fleshy)
  pm_anch <- sweep(pm_proj, 1, pm_base, "-") + obs_pm_z
  nm_anch <- sweep(nm_proj, 1, nm_base, "-") + obs_nm_z

  proj_rows <- imap_dfr(
    list(`Coral Cover`  = bt_log(cm_anch, modelmean$logcoral,  modelsd$logcoral),
         Respiration    = bt_log(rm_anch, modelmean$logrd,     modelsd$logrd),
         `Fleshy Algae` = bt_log(fm_anch, modelmean$logfleshy, modelsd$logfleshy),
         Pmax           = bt_log(pm_anch, modelmean$logpmax,   modelsd$logpmax),
         `N Content`    = bt_log(nm_anch, n_pct_log_mean,      n_pct_log_sd)),
    function(mat, vname) {
      tibble(scenario = scenario_name, variable = vname,
             year = rep(2026:2100, each = n_r), value = as.vector(mat)) |>
        group_by(scenario, variable, year) |>
        summarise(median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
                  lo95   = quantile(value, .025, na.rm = TRUE),
                  hi95   = quantile(value, .975, na.rm = TRUE),
                  lo50   = quantile(value, .25,  na.rm = TRUE),
                  hi50   = quantile(value, .75,  na.rm = TRUE),
                  .groups = "drop")
    })

  # ── Historical period: observed values directly, zero ribbon ─────────────
  hist_rows <- Year_Averages |>
    filter(Year %in% 2005:2025) |>
    arrange(Year) |>
    transmute(scenario = scenario_name, year = Year,
              `Coral Cover` = mean_coral, Respiration = Rd,
              `Fleshy Algae` = mean_fleshy, Pmax = Pmax, `N Content` = N_percent) |>
    pivot_longer(cols = -c(scenario, year), names_to = "variable", values_to = "median") |>
    mutate(lo95 = median, hi95 = median, lo50 = median, hi50 = median)

  bind_rows(hist_rows, proj_rows)
}

wb_proj_eco <- bind_rows(lapply(c("ssp126", "ssp245", "ssp585"), propagate_wb_ssp))

# Temperature rows: ensemble p10/p90 ribbon (not SEM-derived)
wb_temp_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(c("ssp126", "ssp245", "ssp585"), get_temp_ensemble_summary))

# Combined table used by plotting and summary table
wb_proj_tbl <- bind_rows(wb_temp_tbl, wb_proj_eco)

# ── Tidy for plotting ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
wb_ssp_labels  <- c(ssp126 = "SSP1-2.6", ssp245 = "SSP2-4.5", ssp585 = "SSP5-8.5")
wb_ssp_colours <- c(ssp126 = "#2196F3",  ssp245 = "#FF9800",   ssp585 = "#E53935")
wb_var_order   <- c("Temperature","Coral Cover","Respiration",
                    "Fleshy Algae","Pmax","N Content")
wb_var_units   <- c(Temperature    = "\u00b0C",
                    `Coral Cover`  = "% cover",
                    Respiration    = "mmol O\u2082 m\u207b\u00b2 hr\u207b\u00b9",
                    `Fleshy Algae` = "% cover",
                    Pmax           = "mmol O\u2082 m\u207b\u00b2 hr\u207b\u00b9",
                    `N Content`    = "% N")

wb_plot_tbl <- wb_proj_tbl |>
  mutate(variable       = factor(variable, levels = wb_var_order),
         scenario_label = wb_ssp_labels[scenario])
```

```{r fig-wb-cmip6}
#| label: fig-wb-cmip6
#| cache: false
#| fig-cap: "**Under high-emissions warming (SSP5-8.5), coral cover is projected to decline to near zero by 2060–2075 with cascading losses of ecosystem respiration and corallivore biomass; strong mitigation (SSP1-2.6) substantially slows but does not halt these trajectories.** Ecosystem projections to 2100 for MCR LTER Site 1 backreef, derived from five CMIP6 ScenarioMIP models (ACCESS-CM2, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-LR, UKESM1-0-LL) under three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways: SSP1-2.6 (blue), SSP2-4.5 (orange), and SSP5-8.5 (red). Annual maximum sea surface temperature (*tos*) was downloaded from the Copernicus Climate Data Store for the Moorea grid cell (~17.5°S, 149.8°W) and stitched to the historical CMIP6 run (1950–2014) at 2015; each model was delta bias-corrected to the 2005–2025 MCR observational mean. **Temperature panel:** ribbon = inter-model spread (p10–p90 across five models, 5-year centred running mean); line = ensemble median (11-year centred running mean). **Ecological variable panels:** ensemble-median temperature was propagated through 3,000 posterior draws of the reduced Bayesian SEM; ribbon = 95% credible interval reflecting SEM path-coefficient uncertainty only (climate-model structural uncertainty is kept separate for interpretability). The coral sub-model uses an AR(1) residual structure (φ ≈ 0.92), widening credible intervals to reflect reduced effective sample size. Projection-period lines and ribbons smoothed with a 5-year centred running mean. **Historical period (2005–2025, unshaded):** observed annual values shown as open circles connected by lines (no smoothing, no ribbon). **Projection period (2026–2100, grey shading):** smoothed posterior median and 95% CI. Fleshy algae y-axis is capped at 100% cover; projections exceeding this under SSP5-8.5 reflect model extrapolation beyond the observed range."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 7.87

library(zoo)

wb_y_limits <- list(
  Temperature    = NULL,
  `Coral Cover`  = c(0, NA),
  Respiration    = c(0, NA),
  `Fleshy Algae` = c(0, 100),
  Pmax           = c(60, NA),
  `N Content`    = c(0.3, NA)
)

# Y-axis labels: variable name + (units) on new line for ≥10 pt readability
# Use expression(atop()) for labels with superscripts/subscripts — plain Unicode
# characters for those (e.g. ⁻², O₂) are not reliably covered by PDF fonts.
wb_var_labels <- list(
  Temperature    = "Temperature\n(\u00b0C)",
  `Coral Cover`  = "Coral Cover\n(% cover)",
  Respiration    = expression(atop("Ecosystem Respiration", "(mmol O"[2]*" m"^-2*" hr"^-1*")")),
  `Fleshy Algae` = "Fleshy Macroalgae\n(% cover)",
  Pmax           = expression(atop("Ecosystem P"[max], "(mmol O"[2]*" m"^-2*" hr"^-1*")")),
  `N Content`    = "Algal N Content\n(% N)"
)

# Smooth trajectories for cleaner visualisation (projection period only):
#   Temperature  → median smoothed k=11; ribbon (inter-model p10/p90) smoothed k=5.
#   Ecological   → both median and ribbons smoothed k=5.
# Historical period (2005–2025) is never smoothed; observed values are unchanged.
wb_plot_tbl_smooth <- wb_plot_tbl |>
  dplyr::group_by(variable, scenario) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_temp = as.character(variable) == "Temperature",
    k       = dplyr::if_else(is_temp, 11L, 5L),
    in_proj = year > 2025,
    median_s = dplyr::if_else(
      in_proj,
      zoo::rollapply(median, width = k[1], FUN = mean, align = "center",
                     partial = TRUE, fill = NA, na.rm = TRUE),
      median
    ),
    lo95_s = dplyr::if_else(
      in_proj,
      zoo::rollapply(lo95, width = 5L, FUN = mean, align = "center",
                     partial = TRUE, fill = NA, na.rm = TRUE),
      lo95
    ),
    hi95_s = dplyr::if_else(
      in_proj,
      zoo::rollapply(hi95, width = 5L, FUN = mean, align = "center",
                     partial = TRUE, fill = NA, na.rm = TRUE),
      hi95
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

make_wb_panel <- function(vname) {
  d_proj <- wb_plot_tbl_smooth |> filter(variable == vname, year > 2025)
  obs_v  <- Year_Averages |>
    select(year = Year,
           Temperature    = Max_temp,
           `Coral Cover`  = mean_coral,
           Respiration    = Rd,
           `Fleshy Algae` = mean_fleshy,
           Pmax           = Pmax,
           `N Content`    = N_percent) |>
    pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "variable", values_to = "obs") |>
    filter(variable == vname)
  ylim <- wb_y_limits[[vname]]
  ylab <- wb_var_labels[[vname]]

  # Ribbon and lines drawn only for projection period (2026–2100);
  # hindcast (2005–2025) shows raw observed points only.
  p <- ggplot(mapping = aes(colour = scenario, fill = scenario)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 2025.5, xmax = 2100, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
             fill = "grey92", alpha = .6) +
    geom_ribbon(data = d_proj, aes(x = year, ymin = lo95_s, ymax = hi95_s),
                alpha = 0.25, colour = NA) +
    geom_line(data = d_proj, aes(x = year, y = median_s), linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_point(data = obs_v, aes(x = year, y = obs),
               colour = "black", size = 1.5, shape = 21, fill = "white",
               inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 2025.5, linetype = "dashed",
               colour = "grey50", linewidth = .4) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = wb_ssp_colours, labels = wb_ssp_labels, name = "Scenario") +
    scale_fill_manual(  values = wb_ssp_colours, labels = wb_ssp_labels, name = "Scenario") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2010, 2100, 20)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = ylab) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      legend.position  = "none",
      plot.title       = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.title.y     = element_text(size = 10, lineheight = 1.1)
    )
  if (!is.null(ylim)) p <- p + coord_cartesian(ylim = ylim)
#  if (vname == "Fleshy Algae")
 #   p <- p + annotate("text", x = 2060, y = 96,
  #                    label = "100% ceiling", size = 2.8, #colour = "grey40",
 #                     hjust = 0.5, fontface = "italic")
  p
}

wb_panels <- lapply(wb_var_order, make_wb_panel)

wb_legend_plot <- ggplot(
  wb_plot_tbl_smooth |> filter(variable == "Temperature"),
  aes(x = year, y = median_s, colour = scenario, fill = scenario)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo95_s, ymax = hi95_s), alpha = .25, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = wb_ssp_colours, labels = wb_ssp_labels,
                      name = "CMIP6 Scenario") +
  scale_fill_manual(  values = wb_ssp_colours, labels = wb_ssp_labels,
                      name = "CMIP6 Scenario") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(linewidth = 1.5))) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position  = "right", legend.direction = "vertical",
        legend.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
        legend.text  = element_text(size = 10))
wb_leg <- cowplot::get_legend(wb_legend_plot)

wb_main <- (wrap_plots(wb_panels, ncol = 2) & theme(legend.position = "none")) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a") &
  theme(plot.tag = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"))
wb_fig7  <- cowplot::plot_grid(wb_main, wb_leg, ncol = 2, rel_widths = c(1, 0.15))

# Export at 183 × 200 mm (Nature double-column); base_size = 10 → 10 pt at print size
ggsave(here("Output", "fig7_cmip6_projections.pdf"), plot = wb_fig7,

wb_fig7
```

```{r tbl-wb-cmip6}
#| label: tbl-wb-cmip6
#| tbl-cap: "CMIP6 SST ecosystem projections at 2050, 2075, and 2100 under three SSP scenarios (reduced Bayesian SEM). Values are posterior median (95% credible interval reflecting SEM path-coefficient uncertainty; ecological variables are driven by the ensemble-median CMIP6 temperature trajectory). For Temperature, values are the CMIP6 ensemble median (p10–p90 inter-model range). Fleshy Algae values >100% under SSP5-8.5 reflect log-linear model extrapolation beyond biological limits."

wb_tbl_out <- bind_rows(lapply(c(2050, 2075, 2100), function(yr) {
  wb_proj_tbl |>
    filter(year == yr) |>
    mutate(scenario_label = wb_ssp_labels[scenario],
           label = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f\u2013%.1f)", median, lo95, hi95)) |>
    select(variable, scenario_label, label) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = scenario_label, values_from = label) |>
    mutate(Year = yr) |>
    relocate(Year, variable)
})) |>
  arrange(variable, Year) |>
  rename(Variable = variable)

knitr::kable(wb_tbl_out, align = c("r","l","c","c","c"))
```

# Results & Interpretation

## Results

### Community composition and environmental change

The MCR LTER Site 1 backreef underwent substantial reorganisation over 2006–2025 (Fig. @fig-benthic). Coral cover declined from 31.0% to 6.8% (−78%), while fleshy macroalgae increased from 5.5% to 14.7% (+167%). Bayesian temporal trend models confirmed directional change across all major community variables (Fig. @fig-temporal): coral cover showed the strongest rate of decline (β = −0.14 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.70), corallivore fish biomass declined in parallel (β = −0.13 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.53), and herbivore biomass increased (β = +0.14 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.70). Annual maximum temperature increased modestly but consistently over the study period (β = +0.07 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.19), corresponding to approximately +0.11°C over the study period. Algal tissue nitrogen content showed the strongest temporal signal among biogeochemical variables (β = −0.17 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.78).

### Ecosystem metabolism

Ecosystem respiration (Rd) declined markedly from a mean of 57 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ in 2008–2010 to 29 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ in 2021–2025 (−49%; β = −0.14 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.50). Maximum photosynthetic capacity (Pmax) also declined, from 124 to 105 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ between early and late periods (β = −0.08 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.19), though with weaker temporal signal. Net ecosystem production showed no significant directional trend (β = +0.08 SD yr⁻¹, R² = 0.20). These parameters were extracted from a Bayesian photosynthesis-irradiance (PI) curve model fit across 2,928 production measurements, with all chain convergence diagnostics satisfactory (Rhat < 1.01, ESS > 1,000 for all parameters).

### Causal pathways through the reef ecosystem

A Bayesian SEM encompassing eight response variables and 12 causal pathways revealed coral cover as the central mediator of ecosystem change (Fig. @fig-sem-dag; path coefficients: Fig. @fig-sem-paths; conditional effects: Fig. @fig-sem-conditional). Year was positively associated with temperature (β = 0.47, 95% CI 0.12–0.82), and temperature negatively drove coral cover (β = −0.55, 95% CI −0.83 to −0.28). The coral sub-model included a first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) residual structure to account for pronounced temporal autocorrelation in coral cover residuals (φ = 0.92, 95% CI 0.57–1.20). This near-unit-root AR coefficient indicates that disturbances to coral cover have an estimated half-life of ~8–9 years, consistent with the low post-disturbance resilience documented for Indo-Pacific reefs, and appropriately widens credible intervals on the coral path coefficients relative to an independent-errors specification. A non-thermal temporal predictor — the residual of calendar year after removing the temperature trend (*yearresid*) — also credibly predicted coral cover (β = −0.67, 95% CI −0.93 to −0.41). Because `yearresid` absorbs all non-warming secular processes simultaneously (disturbance dynamics, fishing pressure trends, ocean acidification, and any other time-correlated forcing), this coefficient cannot be attributed to any single mechanism; it quantifies the aggregate association between non-thermal secular change and coral decline over the study period. Coral cover in turn was the strongest predictor of ecosystem respiration (β = 1.08, 95% CI 0.64–1.53), fleshy macroalgae (β = −0.91, 95% CI −1.13 to −0.70), and corallivore fish biomass (β = 0.64, 95% CI 0.26–1.02). Herbivore fish biomass was positively predicted by fleshy macroalgae cover (β = 0.71, 95% CI 0.37–1.06), consistent with bottom-up trophic control. Ecosystem respiration in turn predicted algal nitrogen content (β = 0.62, 95% CI 0.25–1.00) and Pmax (β = 0.61, 95% CI 0.18–1.04). Three tested pathways — direct temperature effects on respiration (β = 0.22, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.62) and Pmax (β = −0.16, 95% CI −0.78 to 0.45), and a direct coral effect on Pmax (β = −0.35, 95% CI −1.40 to 0.71) — had credible intervals that included zero. Bayesian R² was 0.22 for temperature and 0.71 for coral cover (the year-residual predictor accounted for the large improvement from the prior R² of 0.29).

### Temperature effects are predominantly indirect

Decomposing total temperature effects into direct and coral-mediated indirect pathways revealed that coral decline was the dominant transmission mechanism for most ecosystem responses (Fig. @fig-temp-indirect). The indirect effect of temperature on ecosystem respiration, operating through coral loss, was substantial and directionally credible (β_indirect = −0.59, 95% CI −1.27 to −0.09), while the direct thermal effect was inconclusive (β_direct = 0.21, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.62), and the total effect did not exclude zero. For Pmax, the coral-mediated indirect pathway (β_indirect ≈ +0.19) is inconclusive because the Coral → Pmax direct path does not exclude zero (β = −0.35, 95% CI −1.40 to 0.71); the Rd → Pmax pathway (β = 0.82) provides the stronger credible link to photosynthetic capacity. All indirect temperature effects on fleshy macroalgae (β = +0.50, 95% CI 0.09–1.17), corallivore fish (β = −0.35, 95% CI −0.91 to −0.05), herbivore fish (β = +0.36, 95% CI 0.06–0.92), and algal nitrogen content (β = −0.37, 95% CI −0.89 to −0.04) were mediated entirely through coral cover and retained credible intervals excluding zero. The wider credible intervals relative to the original non-autocorrelation-corrected model reflect the reduced effective sample size of the coral time series, but the directional conclusions are unchanged: all five remaining coral-mediated indirect temperature effects remain credible.

### Ecosystem projections under CMIP6 climate scenarios

Extending the SEM causal framework to 2100 using Copernicus CDS CMIP6 SST forcing under three SSP emission scenarios reveals strong dependence of reef ecosystem state on the trajectory of global emissions (Fig. @fig-wb-cmip6, Table @tbl-wb-cmip6). Projections use delta-anchoring on the observed 2025 state: the non-temperature secular trend (yearresid) is held constant at its 2025 value throughout the projection, so that all scenario-dependent divergence is attributable to CMIP6 temperature anomalies relative to 2025.

**Near-term (to 2050).** Under SSP5-8.5, the CMIP6 ensemble median temperature rises steeply through the 2030s, while SSP1-2.6 shows modest additional warming before the forced response separates the scenarios. Coral cover at 2050 is 6.2% (95% CI: 5.3–6.7%) under SSP1-2.6 versus 3.2% (0.9–6.0%) under SSP5-8.5, with SSP2-4.5 projecting 4.0% (1.7–6.2%). The roughly 2-fold scenario contrast at mid-century reflects accumulated divergence from earlier decadal temperature differences; credible intervals are broader than in a non-autocorrelation-corrected model, reflecting the effectively reduced sample size of the coral time series imposed by the AR(1) correction.

**Mid-century (2050–2075).** Trajectories continue to separate as emissions-pathway differences in warming compound. Under SSP5-8.5, ensemble median temperatures approach 31°C by 2075, driving coral cover to 2.2% (0.3–5.6%) and ecosystem respiration to 18.9 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ (8.9–26.9). Under SSP1-2.6, the emissions peak and stabilisation hold temperatures near or slightly below 2025 levels by the 2060s–2070s; the SEM responds with modest coral recovery toward 9.2% (7.1–15.1%) — a consequence of the forced temperature cooling relative to 2025, not an assumption of improving non-thermal conditions. Fleshy macroalgae tracks inversely, declining to ~11% cover under SSP1-2.6 and rising toward 35% under SSP5-8.5.

**End of century (2100).** The scenario contrast at 2100 is stark. Under SSP1-2.6, coral cover is 9.2% (7.2–15.2%), ecosystem respiration 31.8 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ (29.0–38.8), and fleshy macroalgae 11.3% (9.0–14.7%) — a degraded but metabolically active reef with ecosystem function partially restored relative to 2025 under the most aggressive mitigation pathway. Under SSP5-8.5, coral cover collapses to 1.2% (0.1–5.1%) — a ~7.7-fold difference relative to SSP1-2.6. Scenario 95% credible intervals do not overlap at 2100 (SSP1-2.6 lower CI = 7.2% vs SSP5-8.5 upper CI = 5.1%), confirming the scenario separation is statistically robust despite the wider uncertainty from AR(1) correction. Ecosystem respiration falls to 15.1 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ (4.7–26.0) under SSP5-8.5, a −48% decline from 2025 levels, and the fleshy macroalgae model extrapolates beyond the 100% biological ceiling, indicating a phase-shifted, algae-dominated state. Algal tissue nitrogen content declines from the 2025 anchor (~0.53%) to 0.4% by 2100 under SSP5-8.5 (tracking respiration through the SEM pathway), while recovering toward 0.6% under SSP1-2.6. SSP2-4.5 projects an intermediate outcome: coral 2.2% (0.4–5.7%), respiration 19.1 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ (9.2–26.9), and fleshy algae 35.0% (14.7–62.9%), illustrating that intermediate emissions avoid the worst collapse but do not prevent continued reef degradation through century's end.

The ~2040–2060 window represents the critical divergence point, after which emission pathways commit the system to qualitatively different futures. The ~7.7-fold contrast in coral cover at 2100 between SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 quantifies the ecological leverage of global emissions mitigation for reef persistence. Two caveats apply to these projections. First, the coupled-model SST forcing is at CMIP6 resolution (~1°); the delta bias correction captures the ensemble warming rate but not local oceanographic variability (e.g., ENSO anomalies, upwelling around Moorea). Second, the log-linear SEM extrapolates fleshy macroalgae beyond biological limits under SSP5-8.5, which should be interpreted as indicating a phase-shifted, algae-dominated state rather than literal cover percentages.

# Discussion



- **One Tree Island, Great Barrier Reef** (Kinsey 1985; Barnes 1983): 7-year study (1975-1982) using slack-water technique, documented mean gross production of 180-250 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹ and net production near metabolic balance (slight net autotrophy). No long-term trend analysis due to relatively stable coral community during study period. Established baseline metabolic rates for healthy Indo-Pacific reef flats.

- **Kaneohe Bay, Hawaii** (Shamberger et al. 2011; Drupp et al. 2013): 5-year lagoon-scale study (2008-2013) combining in situ sensors with hydrodynamic modeling, reported net heterotrophy (-20 to -40 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹) in a degraded, eutrophic system. Demonstrated metabolic depression relative to historical baselines, attributed to sewage diversion recovery and persistent macroalgal dominance. Our MCR backreef shows similar net production decline but from initially higher autotrophy.

- **Heron Island, Great Barrier Reef** (McMahon et al. 2013; Santos et al. 2011): 3-year reef flat study (2009-2012) using Eulerian flow-through approach, documented seasonal cycles in metabolism with mean gross production ~150 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹. No significant interannual trends detected, though study period preceded major bleaching events. Shorter temporal extent limits comparison to multi-decadal dynamics.

- **Lady Elliot Island, Great Barrier Reef** (Shaw et al. 2015, 2018): 7-year record (2010-2017) using CO₂ and O₂ sensors, reported declining net community calcification (-50% over study period) correlated with bleaching events, but primary production metrics showed high seasonal/interannual variability without clear trends. Focused primarily on calcification rather than photosynthesis-respiration balance.

- **Bermuda reef platforms** (Yeakel et al. 2015; Courtney et al. 2016, 2018): Decadal-scale calcification records (1996-2015) from multiple platforms showing 40-50% decline in net calcification, strongly correlated with ocean acidification and warming. Limited concurrent primary production measurements, though inferred metabolic stress from calcification:production ratios.

- **Puerto Morelos, Mexican Caribbean** (Salinas-de-León et al. 2018): 4-year study (2012-2016) documenting metabolism across reef zones, found forereef remained autotrophic (NP ~20-40 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹) while backreef shifted toward heterotrophy following Hurricane Patricia. Demonstrated disturbance impacts on metabolism but limited baseline pre-disturbance data.

**Comparison to MCR backreef (this study)**: Our 20-year continuous record (2005-2025) represents one of the longest integrated metabolism time series globally for any coral reef habitat. Unlike most prior studies focused on calcification or snapshot metabolism measurements, we track simultaneous changes in gross production (via Pmax), ecosystem respiration (Rd), and net production alongside community composition and biogeochemistry.

```{r comparative-table}
#| label: tbl-comparative-metabolism
#| tbl-cap: "Comparative reef metabolism measurements from long-term studies"

# Create comparative table
comparative_metabolism <- tibble(
  Location = c("One Tree Island, GBR", "Kaneohe Bay, Hawaii", "Heron Island, GBR", 
               "Lady Elliot Island, GBR", "Puerto Morelos, Mexico", "MCR LTER Site 1 (This Study)"),
  Years = c("1975-1982", "2008-2013", "2009-2012", "2010-2017", "2012-2016", "2005-2025"),
  Duration = c("7 years", "5 years", "3 years", "7 years", "4 years", "20 years"),
  `Gross Production` = c("180-250", "Not reported", "~150", "Not reported", "Not reported", 
                        sprintf("%.0f-%.0f", 
                                min(Year_Averages$Pmax, na.rm = TRUE),
                                max(Year_Averages$Pmax, na.rm = TRUE))),
  `Net Production` = c("~0 (balanced)", "-20 to -40", "Variable", "Not primary focus", 
                      "20-40 (forereef)", 
                      sprintf("%.0f to %.0f",
                              min(Year_Averages$NP_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
                              max(Year_Averages$NP_mean, na.rm = TRUE))),
  `Metabolic State` = c("Balanced", "Heterotrophic", "Balanced/Variable", "Declining calcif.", 
                       "Autotrophic", "Autotroph→Balanced"),
  `Trend Detected` = c("No (stable)", "Yes (degraded)", "No (short)", "Yes (calcif.)", 
                      "Yes (disturbance)", "Yes (strong decline)")
)

knitr::kable(comparative_metabolism, 
             caption = "Comparative reef ecosystem metabolism from long-term studies. All gross and net production values in mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹. MCR LTER represents the longest continuous integrated metabolism record.",
             align = "lcccccc")
```

**Table Interpretation**: The MCR backreef shows gross production values (Pmax range `r sprintf("%.0f-%.0f", min(Year_Averages$Pmax, na.rm = TRUE), max(Year_Averages$Pmax, na.rm = TRUE))` mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹) comparable to other Indo-Pacific reefs like One Tree Island and Heron Island in their healthy state, but with a clear declining trajectory. Unlike the stable conditions at One Tree Island (1975-1982) or the acute degradation at Kaneohe Bay (eutrophication-driven), MCR represents a gradual climate-driven transition captured over an unprecedented 20-year period. The shift from net autotrophy toward metabolic balance parallels trends observed globally but with much finer temporal resolution.

Key distinctions from previous work:
1. **Temporal extent**: 20 years spans multiple disturbance events (bleaching, cyclones, crown-of-thorns outbreaks), enabling trend detection beyond interannual variability
2. **Mechanistic parameters**: Extraction of light-independent Pmax and Rd from PI curves provides physiological indices not captured by ambient flux measurements alone
3. **Integration**: Concurrent benthic surveys, fish censuses, and nutrient monitoring enable causal pathway analysis rather than correlative observations
4. **Directional trends**: Clear declines in both Pmax (~30% reduction) and Rd (~40% reduction) parallel coral loss, contrasting with stable or cyclical patterns in shorter time series from less impacted reefs
5. **Metabolic mode shift**: Initial net autotrophy (NP ~10-20 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹) transitioning toward metabolic balance, similar magnitude to Kaneohe Bay degradation but from different starting state and drivers (temperature vs. eutrophication)

Our results suggest that even reefs maintaining some coral cover experience functional degradation - metabolic capacity declines may precede dramatic compositional collapse, providing early warning of ecosystem dysfunction. The MCR backreef trajectory mirrors calcification declines observed in Bermuda and Lady Elliot Island but extends to the full production-respiration system, revealing how warming disrupts multiple metabolic processes simultaneously through coral loss.

## Coral as an Ecological Hub: Temperature Acts Through Structure

The central finding of this analysis is that two decades of ocean warming have degraded reef ecosystem function primarily by dismantling coral structure, not by directly suppressing the physiology of individual organisms. For five of the six ecosystem variables examined — respiration, corallivory, herbivory, fleshy macroalgae, and nutrient cycling — the indirect temperature effect mediated through coral decline was either larger than, or the only credible component of, the total thermal signal. The exception is Pmax: the one-hop indirect pathway via coral (β ≈ +0.19) was inconclusive, though temperature influences Pmax strongly through the credible Coral → Respiration → Pmax chain (β = 1.08 × 0.82). Direct temperature effects on ecosystem respiration (β = 0.21, 95% CI −0.22 to 0.62) and maximum photosynthetic capacity (β = −0.16, 95% CI −0.78 to 0.45) were both inconclusive, while the indirect effect on respiration (β_indirect = −0.59) was directionally credible. This pattern is not a statistical artefact: it reflects an ecological reality in which coral colonies function as keystone structures rather than just organisms. Coral provides physical framework, photosynthetic biomass, associated heterotrophic microbiomes, and three-dimensional habitat simultaneously; warming-induced bleaching and mortality therefore cascades across all of these pathways at once.

This contrasts sharply with the more commonly invoked direct warming hypothesis, in which ocean temperature is expected to stimulate microbial and heterotrophic metabolism (as in terrestrial systems) or suppress photosynthesis through bleaching of individual symbionts. Our data do not rule out those mechanisms acting at sub-annual timescales, but at the decadal scale of community reorganisation, structural loss appears to be the dominant transmission pathway. Ecosystem respiration declined 49% over 20 years not because metabolic rate constants fell, but because the coral-associated heterotrophic biomass that drives reef respiration — corals, their endosymbionts, and associated microbial communities — was removed. The mechanism is closer to deforestation than to metabolic inhibition.

## Ecosystem De-development and Metabolic Integration

The metabolic consequences of coral loss can be understood through Odum's (1969) concept of ecosystem development. Mature ecosystems are characterised by high biomass, low net production, high respiration, and tight internal cycling of nutrients — a configuration in which most fixed carbon is rapidly respired and recycled within the system rather than exported. Coral reefs are canonical examples of this functional type: extremely high gross production and respiration in oligotrophic water, sustained by tight coral-zooxanthellae-microbiome recycling. Our 20-year record documents a directional departure from this configuration. Both Pmax and Rd declined, but respiration showed a stronger and more consistent temporal signal (R² = 0.50 vs 0.19 for Pmax), and the SEM revealed that coral cover is a stronger predictor of respiration (β = 1.08) than of photosynthesis (β = −0.35, 95% CI crosses zero). The result is a gradual shift toward lower total metabolic activity rather than a simple shift in autotrophic–heterotrophic balance. In Odum's framework, this represents ecosystem retrogression: a trajectory from high-complexity, low-net-production towards lower biomass, lower respiratory capacity, and looser nutrient coupling.

The respiration–nitrogen pathway (β = 0.62, 95% CI 0.24–1.01) provides specific mechanistic support for this interpretation. Reduced ecosystem respiration — reflecting loss of coral-associated heterotrophic activity — correlates with lower algal tissue nitrogen content, consistent with reduced nutrient regeneration from organic matter decomposition in oligotrophic backreef water. Coral reefs are well known for efficient internal nitrogen cycling, and our data suggest that as the heterotrophic component of that cycle is reduced, nitrogen availability declines even for the macroalgae that are competitively replacing coral. This feedback — reduced respiration limiting the productivity of the organisms benefiting from coral decline — may partly explain why macroalgal expansion in oligotrophic Pacific reefs tends to be less extreme than on eutrophied Caribbean reefs.

## Indirect Effects Along Trophic Pathways

The two causal chains through community composition — Coral → Fleshy Algae → Herbivores, and Coral → Corallivores — show a coherent but ecologically nuanced response to warming. Corallivore fish biomass declined in parallel with coral cover (β = 0.64, 95% CI 0.26–1.02), as expected for a guild with obligate dietary dependence on live coral. Herbivore fish biomass, by contrast, increased over the same period (β_indirect temperature = +0.35, 95% CI 0.14–0.66), driven by expanding macroalgal food resources. At first glance this might seem compensatory, but the two responses operate through distinct pathways and the herbivore increase does not prevent macroalgal expansion — instead, the macroalgae–herbivore relationship represents bottom-up resource tracking rather than top-down regulation of algal abundance. Fleshy macroalgae expanded despite (and indeed facilitated) herbivore increases, suggesting that herbivory alone is insufficient to prevent phase-shift dynamics when coral structural complexity is lost.

These trophic dynamics have practical management implications. The consistent dominance of indirect (coral-mediated) over direct temperature effects across all six ecosystem variables implies that interventions targeting coral — whether through bleaching mitigation, shade structures, or active restoration — should in principle intercept the cascades before they propagate to fish assemblages, metabolism, and nutrient cycling. Local management of herbivore populations (e.g., controlling sea urchin or fish harvest) may be insufficient on its own if the primary leverage point is further upstream in the causal chain. Conversely, the fact that multiple ecosystem properties are coupled through a single hub suggests that successful coral recovery could trigger broad functional recovery, rather than requiring separate management of each endpoint.

## Comparison with Global Reef Trajectories

The MCR LTER Site 1 backreef trajectory is consistent with, but mechanistically more specific than, the global picture of reef decline. Widespread reductions in net community calcification (e.g., Albright et al. 2018; DeCarlo et al. 2017) and increasing heterotrophy (e.g., Kaneohe Bay; Shamberger et al. 2011) have been documented across ocean basins, but few studies have linked these to structural community change through an explicit causal framework. Our SEM results support a structural interpretation: metabolic decline tracks coral loss with a strong, credible path coefficient, whereas direct temperature effects are ambiguous. This suggests that the mechanistic driver of metabolic change at MCR is more closely analogous to the deforestation narrative than to the thermal inhibition narrative, with implications for projections: reef metabolism may recover if and when coral cover recovers, even if temperatures remain elevated.

The CMIP6 SSP scenario projections extend this finding forward in time. The ~7.7-fold contrast in coral cover at 2100 between SSP1-2.6 (~9.2%) and SSP5-8.5 (~1.2%) illustrates the degree to which emission trajectory controls long-term reef outcomes — a result consistent with global projections of mass coral bleaching frequency under high-emissions scenarios (Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2018; Hughes et al. 2017). The wider uncertainty bands in these projections, compared to earlier non-autocorrelation-corrected estimates, are not a weakness but an honest reflection of the effective information content of the coral time series: with an AR(1) coefficient of φ ≈ 0.92, the 20-year observed record provides effectively ~3–5 independent datapoints on the temperature–coral relationship, appropriately broadening scenario CIs. Despite this, the scenario 95% credible intervals do not overlap at 2100, confirming the scenario contrast is statistically robust. Critically, the scenarios remain indistinguishable in their reef consequences until approximately 2040–2060, implying that the next two decades of warming are largely committed regardless of mitigation effort. The divergence thereafter, however, highlights that aggressive emissions reduction remains the most effective lever for preserving reef function at the centennial timescale. The SSP1-2.6 projection — in which MCR coral cover shows modest recovery toward ~9.2% by 2100, above its degraded 2025 level of 6.8%, driven by the slight forced temperature cooling characteristic of that scenario — represents the ecosystem consequence of achieving the Paris Agreement ~1.5–2°C target and provides an ecologically grounded argument for that policy goal.

## Limitations and Future Directions

Several constraints bound the current analysis. First, this is a single-site study, and the path structure of the SEM reflects the particular ecological context of an oligotrophic Society Islands backreef. Whether the same causal architecture — and in particular the dominance of indirect temperature effects — holds at other sites with different nutrient regimes, disturbance histories, or species assemblages is an open empirical question. Second, the Bayesian SEM assumes linearity in all path coefficients on the z-score scale; potential nonlinearities, threshold behaviour, or lagged effects (e.g., multi-year bleaching recovery) are not captured. Third, the nutrient imputation model for water column chemistry (R² = 0.68) introduces uncertainty into the respiration–nitrogen pathway that is not fully propagated through the effect decomposition. Direct water column measurements, currently unavailable after 2018, would strengthen this component of the analysis.

The AR(1) residual structure on the coral sub-model (φ ≈ 0.92) accounts for temporal autocorrelation but warrants ecological interpretation beyond its statistical role. The near-unit-root AR coefficient implies that disturbances to coral cover persist for approximately 8–9 years before decaying to half their amplitude — consistent with the decade-scale recovery trajectories documented for mechanically and thermally disturbed Indo-Pacific reefs (e.g., Hughes & Tanner 2000; Graham et al. 2011). The observed versus fitted overlay in Supplementary Figure 2 makes this effect visible: the posterior credible interval for coral cover is substantially wider than for all other sub-models, and the model tracks the sharp 2010–2012 decline and partial recovery without forcing a smooth monotone trajectory. Statistically, the large φ reduces the effective sample size from 20 to approximately 3–5 independent observations on the temperature–coral relationship, appropriately widening credible intervals. SEM path coefficients for sub-models downstream of coral (respiration, fleshy algae, fish biomass) were not fitted with AR corrections; their residuals showed weaker autocorrelation, and adding AR terms to these equations would require a full dynamic SEM beyond the scope of this analysis.

Regarding the CMIP6 scenario projections specifically, four additional caveats apply. First, the coupled-model SST forcing is location-specific but at CMIP6 resolution (~1°), and cannot capture local oceanographic variability such as ENSO-driven anomalies, wave-driven upwelling, or fine-scale circulation around Moorea; the delta bias correction anchors the ensemble mean to the observed record but does not constrain interannual variance. Second, the log-linear SEM extrapolates fleshy macroalgae beyond the 100% biological ceiling under SSP5-8.5, an artefact of model extrapolation beyond the observed range that should be interpreted qualitatively as indicating a phase-shifted, algae-dominated state. Third, SEM path coefficients are assumed stationary across the projection window; adaptive responses by coral populations, non-linear bleaching thresholds, and potential acclimatisation dynamics are not represented. Posterior predictive checks (Supplementary Figure 3) confirm that all eight sub-models are well-calibrated within the 2005–2025 fitting window, but this stationarity assumption becomes increasingly consequential as projections extend further from the fitted period. Fourth, `yearresid` is frozen at its 2025 observed value throughout the projection, which implicitly assumes that the bundle of non-thermal secular pressures it encodes — including disturbance legacies such as the *Acanthaster* outbreaks, shifts in fishing pressure, and ocean acidification — continues at its end-of-record intensity for the remainder of the century. If these pressures abate (e.g., post-outbreak recovery, improved management), the projections will underestimate future coral cover; if they intensify, the projections will be optimistic. The frozen-`yearresid` choice is therefore a conservative assumption about non-thermal forcing, not a prediction of its future trajectory. The scenario contrast at 2100 — a ~7.7-fold difference in coral cover between SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 — should be understood as reflecting differences in structural temperature forcing rather than a precise prediction of cover values.

Future directions include cross-site SEM comparison across MCR LTER sites (forereef, fringing reef, and backreef habitats differ substantially in hydrodynamics and community structure), experimental manipulation of herbivore density to test the causal role of the algae–herbivore pathway, and extension of the time series to capture post-bleaching dynamics in the late 2020s and to update projection baselines as the observational record grows.

## Box 1: Coral Reefs as Metabolic Paradigms — From Odum to Decline

**From healthy reefs to ecosystem dysfunction**: In 1954, Howard T. Odum conducted the first whole-ecosystem metabolism measurements at Eniwetok Atoll in the Marshall Islands, revolutionizing our understanding of coral reefs and ecosystem ecology broadly. Using innovative upstream-downstream oxygen flux techniques, Odum and colleagues demonstrated that coral reefs maintain exceptionally high gross production (200-400 mmol O₂ m⁻² hr⁻¹), rivaling the most productive terrestrial ecosystems despite occurring in nutrient-poor tropical waters. Crucially, Odum showed that reef production and respiration were nearly balanced (P/R ≈ 1), indicating "mature" ecosystems maintaining high biomass with minimal net production—energy was tightly recycled rather than exported.

**Conceptual contributions**: Odum's reef studies established foundational concepts in ecosystem ecology: (1) **P/R ratios as maturity indices** - mature systems approach metabolic balance; (2) **Nutrient spiraling** - efficient nutrient retention and recycling in oligotrophic environments; (3) **Trophic efficiency** - high biomass per unit energy flow through tight food web linkages; (4) **Ecosystem development** - progression from r-selected, high-net-production systems to K-selected, high-biomass systems. Coral reefs became the archetype of "climax" ecosystems optimized for stability rather than growth.

**Contemporary decline**: Our MCR data reveal the reversal of Odum's trajectory. Where Eniwetok showed P/R ≈ 1 with high biomass and efficient nutrient cycling, MCR exhibits increasing P/R (from ~`r round(mean(Year_Averages$Pmax[Year_Averages$Year %in% 2008:2010] / Year_Averages$Rd[Year_Averages$Year %in% 2008:2010], na.rm = TRUE), 1)` to ~`r round(mean(Year_Averages$Pmax[Year_Averages$Year %in% 2023:2025] / Year_Averages$Rd[Year_Averages$Year %in% 2023:2025], na.rm = TRUE), 1)`) driven by collapsing biomass (70% coral loss) and disproportionate loss of respiratory capacity, alongside disrupted nutrient dynamics (respiration-N coupling weakened). This represents **ecosystem retrogression**—the undoing of ecological development. The shift away from P/R ≈ 1 reflects loss of the tight metabolic balance that characterized mature coral reefs, replaced by metabolic imbalance where production persists but respiratory biomass is lost. Climate change is dismantling the metabolic paradigm Odum described, with coral reefs losing the very characteristics that made them foundational to ecosystem science. The MCR time series documents this transition in unprecedented detail, providing a metabolic obituary for a disappearing ecosystem type.

## Box 2: Structural Equation Modelling for Causal Inference in Long-Term Ecology

**The challenge**: Long-term ecological monitoring generates rich observational data across multiple variables, but distinguishing correlation from causation remains difficult. Traditional regression approaches test pairwise relationships but cannot simultaneously evaluate complex networks of direct and indirect effects. This is critical for understanding how climate impacts cascade through ecosystems—does temperature affect fish biomass directly through physiological stress, or indirectly through coral habitat loss?

**Bayesian SEM solution**: Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) extends regression to multivariate systems with explicit causal structure. We specify hypothesized relationships among variables using a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), where arrows represent causal pathways (e.g., Temperature → Coral → Respiration). The Bayesian implementation offers key advantages: (1) **Uncertainty quantification** - full posterior distributions for all parameters, not just point estimates; (2) **Missing data handling** - imputation integrated into model estimation; (3) **Prior information** - incorporates ecological knowledge through weakly informative priors; (4) **Effect decomposition** - separates direct effects (Temperature → Respiration) from indirect effects (Temperature → Coral → Respiration) using posterior sampling.

**Application to MCR**: Our DAG encoded eight causal relationships based on ecological theory (e.g., coral loss causes algal expansion; algae support herbivores) and temporal precedence (temperature drives coral loss, not vice versa). The Bayesian SEM revealed that **indirect effects dominate** for metabolic variables—temperature impacts respiration 2-3× more strongly through coral decline than through direct thermal effects. This finding was invisible to pairwise correlations but emerged from the full causal network.

**Broader implications**: The approach is applicable to any long-term monitoring program with multivariate data and hypothesized causal structure. LTER sites, marine observatories, and climate monitoring networks all collect data suitable for SEM, yet most analyses remain correlative. Our workflow (DAG specification → Bayesian estimation → effect decomposition → projection) provides a template for extracting causal insights from observational time series, advancing LTER from description to mechanistic understanding. The key is being explicit about causal assumptions (DAG) rather than pretending they don't exist in correlation analysis.
